questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(1) - Woman Director Mandate
questions.question: Aman Steels Ltd., an unlisted public company, has a paid-up share capital of ₹80 Crores and an annual turnover of ₹320 Crores as per its latest audited financial statements for FY 2023-24. On June 15, 2024, the sole woman director resigned due to personal reasons. What is the statutory time limit by which the company must fill the intermittent vacancy under Section 149(1) read with Rule 3 of the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014?
options: At the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of vacancy, whichever is later.
Within 30 days from the date of resignation submitted by the woman director.
Within 6 months from the date of vacancy as per the General Circular of MCA.
At the immediate next Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the company.
questions.ref: Section 149(1) second proviso read with Rule 3 of Companies (Appointment & Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014
questions.explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 149(1) and Rule 3, every listed company and every unlisted public company having paid-up share capital ≥ ₹100 Crore OR turnover ≥ ₹300 Crore must have at least one woman director. Since turnover is ₹320 Cr, the rule applies. Any intermittent vacancy must be filled by the Board at the earliest but not later than immediate next Board meeting or 3 months from the date of such vacancy, whichever is later.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 149(4) & 149(6) - Independent Director Qualification & Tenure
questions.question: Mr. Rajan was appointed as an Independent Director of Trident Pharma Ltd. for a term of 5 consecutive years commencing April 1, 2019. In July 2023, his son was appointed as a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a subsidiary company of Trident Pharma Ltd. Trident Pharma Ltd. now proposes to re-appoint Mr. Rajan for a second consecutive term of 5 years with effect from April 1, 2024. Which of the following statements is legally correct under Section 149(6)?
options: Mr. Rajan is disqualified from being appointed as an Independent Director because his relative (son) holds the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (CFO) in a subsidiary company during the preceding three financial years.
Mr. Rajan can be re-appointed by passing an Ordinary Resolution in general meeting without any impediment since the son is in a subsidiary, not the holding company.
Mr. Rajan can only be appointed if approval from the Central Government (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) is obtained prior to general meeting.
The restriction on relatives being KMP applies only to spouse and parents, not sons or daughters under the definition of relative in Section 2(77).
questions.ref: Section 149(6)(e)(i) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 149(6)(e)(i), a person is not eligible to be an Independent Director if none of his relatives holds or has held the position of a Key Managerial Personnel (KMP) or is or has been employee of the company or its holding, subsidiary or associate company in any of the three financial years immediately preceding the financial year in which he is proposed to be appointed. Since the son is a KMP (CFO) in a subsidiary, Mr. Rajan ceases to meet the independence criteria.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 164(2) - Disqualification of Directors for Company Default
questions.question: Apex Motors Ltd. failed to file its financial statements and annual returns for three continuous financial years (FY 2020-21, 2021-22, and 2022-23) with the Registrar of Companies. Mr. Vikram was appointed as an additional director on the Board of Apex Motors Ltd. on December 1, 2023. On January 10, 2024, another company, Zenith Infotech Ltd., where Mr. Vikram was already a director, intends to re-appoint him at its AGM. Under Section 164(2) proviso, what is the status of Mr. Vikram's disqualification?
options: Mr. Vikram shall not incur disqualification under Section 164(2) in Zenith Infotech Ltd. for a period of six months from the date of his appointment in Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram incurs immediate automatic disqualification under Section 164(2) for 5 years across all companies from the moment he joined Apex Motors Ltd.
Mr. Vikram is disqualified for lifetime from being appointed as director in any public company unless compounded by NCLT.
Disqualification under Section 164(2) applies only to Managing Directors and Whole-Time Directors, exempting Additional Directors.
questions.ref: Section 164(2) proviso (inserted by Companies (Amendment) Act, 2017)
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 164(2), where a person is appointed as a director of a company which is in default of clause (a) or clause (b) of subsection (2), he shall not incur the disqualification for a period of six months from the date of his appointment. This provides a 6-month grace period for newly appointed directors to rectify defaults.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 165 - Maximum Number of Directorships
questions.question: Ms. Shalini currently holds directorships in 18 companies, comprising 8 public companies and 10 private companies. Two of the private companies are dormant companies under Section 455, and one is a Section 8 non-profit company. She is now offered an alternate directorship in an unlisted public company. Can Ms. Shalini accept this new directorship without violating Section 165?
options: Yes, because dormant companies and Section 8 companies are excluded from the ceiling of 20 total companies and 10 public companies under Section 165, and alternate directorship is counted towards the ceiling.
No, because alternate directorships cannot be counted under any circumstances under the Companies Act, 2013.
No, because a person can never hold directorship in more than 10 companies of any class under the revised MCA norms.
Yes, but only if prior approval of the Central Government is obtained through Form DIR-12.
questions.ref: Section 165(1) read with Explanation I & II of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 165(1), the maximum number of directorships is 20, of which public companies cannot exceed 10. Directorship in a dormant company (Sec 455) and Section 8 company are excluded from the limit. Alternate directorship is explicitly included in calculating limits. Here: Active public companies = 8 (+1 proposed = 9 ≤ 10); Active total = 8 public + 8 active private = 16 (+1 = 17 ≤ 20). Hence, she can legally accept.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 173 - Board Meetings & Quorum for Interested Directors
questions.question: The Board of Directors of Pioneer Infrastructure Ltd. consists of 9 directors. At a meeting convened to consider a commercial contract involving an entity in which 7 directors are interested under Section 184(2), only 2 non-interested directors are present in person. What constitutes a valid quorum for transacting this specific business under Section 174(3)?
options: The quorum shall be the number of non-interested directors who are present at the meeting being not less than two.
A minimum of one-third of the total strength (i.e., 3 directors) is mandatory; hence the meeting must be adjourned for want of quorum.
All 7 interested directors can vote after making an oral disclosure of interest in the meeting.
The contract must be referred directly to the Central Government since quorum cannot be formed.
questions.ref: Section 174(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 174(3), where at any time the number of interested directors exceeds or is equal to two-thirds of the total strength of the Board, the number of directors who are not interested and present at the meeting, being not less than two, shall be the quorum during such time for that business. Here 7 out of 9 are interested (≥ 2/3rd = 6); the 2 disinterested directors present constitute valid quorum.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 177 - Audit Committee Mandatory Constitution & Functions
questions.question: Kiran Fabricators Ltd., an unlisted public company, has paid-up share capital of ₹8 Crores, turnover of ₹85 Crores, and outstanding bank borrowings and debentures aggregating ₹120 Crores. Is the company required to constitute an Audit Committee under Section 177 read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because its outstanding loans, borrowings, debentures or deposits exceed ₹50 Crores.
No, because paid-up capital is below ₹10 Crores and turnover is below ₹100 Crores.
No, constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory only for equity-listed public companies.
Yes, but only if at least 100 members requisition the Board in writing.
questions.ref: Section 177(1) read with Rule 4 of Companies (Meetings of Board & Powers) Rules, 2014
questions.explanation: Under Rule 4, the Board of every unlisted public company having: (a) paid-up capital ≥ ₹10 Cr; OR (b) turnover ≥ ₹100 Cr; OR (c) outstanding loans, debentures, deposits > ₹50 Cr, must constitute an Audit Committee. Since borrowings/debentures are ₹120 Cr (> ₹50 Cr), constitution of Audit Committee is mandatory.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 185 - Loans to Directors & Controlled Entities
questions.question: Solaris Power Ltd. desires to advance a loan of ₹15 Crores to Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Mr. Arvind is a director of Solaris Power Ltd. and holds 28% of the total voting power in Helios Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. Under the amended Section 185, under what conditions can Solaris Power Ltd. advance this loan?
options: A special resolution must be passed in general meeting with explanatory statement disclosing full particulars, and the borrowing company must utilise the loan exclusively for its principal business activities.
The loan is completely prohibited under Section 185(1) as loans to any entity where a director holds >20% voting power cannot be given under any circumstances.
Only an ordinary resolution in Board meeting is required with the consent of all directors present.
The loan can be given only with prior approval of NCLT and Reserve Bank of India.
questions.ref: Section 185(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 185(2), a company may advance any loan or give guarantee/security to any person in whom any of the directors is interested (which includes a private company where a director holds ≥25% voting power) provided: (a) a special resolution is passed in general meeting; and (b) the loans are utilised by the borrowing company for its principal business activities.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 186 - Loans & Investments by Company
questions.question: Blue Horizon Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹50 Crores, free reserves of ₹30 Crores, and securities premium account of ₹20 Crores. The Board of Directors wishes to grant a loan of ₹65 Crores to a business partner firm. What is the statutory requirement under Section 186(3) for giving this loan?
options: Prior approval by Special Resolution in general meeting is mandatory, because the aggregate loan exceeds 60% of paid-up capital, free reserves & securities premium (60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr) and 100% of free reserves & securities premium (₹50 Cr).
Only unanimous Board resolution is sufficient as the amount is less than 100% of paid-up capital.
Ordinary resolution in AGM is sufficient with prior sanction of ROC.
No resolution is needed if the rate of interest is higher than the bank rate.
questions.ref: Section 186(2) and 186(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 186(2), a company cannot directly or indirectly give loan/guarantee/security exceeding 60% of (Paid-up capital + Free reserves + Securities premium) OR 100% of (Free reserves + Securities premium), whichever is more, without prior approval by special resolution. Here: 60% of ₹100 Cr = ₹60 Cr; 100% of ₹50 Cr = ₹50 Cr. Threshold = ₹60 Cr. Since proposed loan is ₹65 Cr (> ₹60 Cr), prior Special Resolution is required.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 188 - Related Party Transactions & Threshold Limits
questions.question: Sigma Electronics Ltd., a public company, proposes to enter into a contract for sale of manufactured goods amounting to ₹120 Crores to Delta Components Pvt. Ltd., an entity where the Managing Director of Sigma holds 30% shares. The annual turnover of Sigma Electronics Ltd. as per its latest audited balance sheet is ₹900 Crores. Does this transaction require prior approval by Ordinary Resolution under Section 188 read with Rule 15?
options: Yes, because the contract value of ₹120 Crores exceeds 10% of the annual turnover of the company (10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr).
No, approval of shareholders is needed only if contract value exceeds ₹100 Crores regardless of turnover.
No, only Audit Committee approval is needed; shareholder resolution is never required for sale of goods.
Yes, but it requires a Special Resolution passed with 75% majority, not an Ordinary Resolution.
questions.ref: Section 188(1) read with Rule 15(3) of Companies (Meetings of Board and its Powers) Rules, 2014
questions.explanation: Under Rule 15(3)(a)(i), contracts or arrangements with respect to sale, purchase or supply of any goods or materials directly or through appointment of agent exceeding 10% of turnover requires prior approval of the company by ordinary resolution. 10% of ₹900 Cr = ₹90 Cr. Since ₹120 Cr > ₹90 Cr, prior ordinary resolution in general meeting is required.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 197 & Schedule V - Managerial Remuneration Limits
questions.question: Quantum Infotech Ltd., a public company with 3 whole-time directors and 1 managing director, has earned a net profit of ₹40 Crores computed under Section 198 for FY 2023-24. What is the maximum managerial remuneration payable to all managerial personnel without seeking approval of the Central Government?
options: 10% of net profits (₹4.0 Crores) if there is more than one such director, and overall 11% of net profits (₹4.4 Crores) for all directors including non-executive directors.
5% of net profits regardless of the number of whole-time directors.
15% of net profits provided unanimous consent of the Board of Directors is obtained.
Unlimited remuneration provided an ordinary resolution is passed in the Annual General Meeting.
questions.ref: Section 197(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 197(1), total managerial remuneration payable by a public company to its directors shall not exceed 11% of net profits. Remuneration payable to any one managing director or whole-time director shall not exceed 5% of net profits, and if there is more than one such director, remuneration shall not exceed 10% of net profits to all of them together. Beyond 11%, a special resolution is required.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 203 - Mandatory Appointment of KMP
questions.question: Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has a paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores and turnover of ₹80 Crores. Is Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. mandatorily required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary under Section 203 read with Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014?
options: Yes, because every private company having a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more is required to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary.
No, mandatory appointment of KMP applies exclusively to listed public companies.
No, the threshold for private companies was raised to ₹50 Crores in the recent MCA amendment.
Yes, but only if the company has more than 200 employees on its payroll.
questions.ref: Rule 8A of Companies (Appointment and Remuneration of Managerial Personnel) Rules, 2014
questions.explanation: Under Rule 8A (as amended w.e.f. April 1, 2020), every private company which has a paid-up share capital of ₹10 Crores or more shall have a whole-time company secretary. Since Zenith Retail Pvt. Ltd. has paid-up share capital of ₹12 Crores (≥ ₹10 Cr), it must appoint a whole-time CS.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Companies Act, 2013: incorporation, management, meetings, and compliance
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 101 & 103 - Notice of General Meeting & Quorum
questions.question: A public company having 4,500 members convenes an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM). At the appointed time, only 12 members are personally present. After waiting for 30 minutes, 14 members are personally present. What is the legal consequence regarding quorum under Section 103?
options: The meeting stands adjourned to the same day in the next week at the same time and place, because the required quorum for a company having between 1,000 and 5,000 members is 15 members personally present.
The 14 members present constitute valid quorum since the shortfall is less than 10%.
The meeting is immediately dissolved as an EGM cannot be adjourned under any circumstances.
The Chairman can use his casting vote to declare quorum validly established.
questions.ref: Section 103(1)(a) and 103(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 103(1)(a), for a public company: (i) 5 members personally present if members ≤ 1,000; (ii) 15 members if members > 1,000 but ≤ 5,000; (iii) 30 members if members > 5,000. Here members = 4,500, so quorum is 15 members personally present. Since only 14 were present within 30 minutes, the meeting stands adjourned to next week unless called by requisitionists.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 271 - Grounds for Winding Up by Tribunal
questions.question: Under Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013 (as amended by IBC 2016), which of the following is NOT a permissible ground for the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) to order the winding up of a company?
options: Inability of the company to pay its debts upon receipt of a statutory demand notice from an operational creditor.
The company has acted against the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, or public order.
The Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.
The company has made a default in filing with the Registrar its financial statements or annual returns for immediately preceding five consecutive financial years.
questions.ref: Section 271 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Schedule XI)
questions.explanation: Under Section 271 as amended by IBC 2016, 'inability to pay debts' was deleted from Section 271 and shifted exclusively to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (CIRP). The remaining grounds under Sec 271 are: special resolution, acting against sovereignty/integrity of India, fraudulent conduct (Sec 213), default in filing financial statements/annual returns for 5 consecutive years, and just and equitable ground.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 272 - Petitioners for Winding Up
questions.question: A petition for winding up of Mayur Finlease Ltd. is presented before the NCLT by the Registrar of Companies on the ground that the company has defaulted in filing its financial statements for 5 consecutive financial years. Under Section 272(3), what condition precedent must be satisfied by the Registrar before presenting this petition?
options: The Registrar must obtain previous sanction of the Central Government, and the Central Government shall not accord sanction without giving the company a reasonable opportunity of making representations.
The Registrar must obtain approval of at least 75% of the secured creditors of the company.
The Registrar must publish a notice in the Official Gazette at least 90 days before filing.
No sanction is required if default exceeds 3 years.
questions.ref: Section 272(3) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 272(3), the Registrar shall not present a petition on any grounds specified in subsection (1) except on the ground specified in clause (b) or (d) or (e) of Section 271, and only after obtaining the previous sanction of the Central Government. The Central Government shall not accord sanction without giving the company a reasonable opportunity of making representations.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 281 - Submission of Report by Company Liquidator
questions.question: The NCLT passes a winding up order appointing Mr. Deshmukh as the Company Liquidator of Falcon Engineering Ltd. Under Section 281(1), within what timeframe from the date of the winding up order must the Company Liquidator submit a preliminary report to the Tribunal?
options: Within 60 days from the date of the winding up order.
Within 30 days from the date of his appointment.
Within 180 days from the date of admission of the petition.
Within 1 year from the date of receipt of the statement of affairs.
questions.ref: Section 281(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 281(1), where the Tribunal has made a winding up order or appointed a Company Liquidator, such liquidator shall, within 60 days from the date of the order, submit to the Tribunal a report containing particulars of assets, cash, debts, liabilities, and failure causes.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 326 & 327 - Overriding Preferential Payments (Workmen Dues)
questions.question: In the winding up of Premier Textiles Ltd., the assets realize ₹10 Crores. The claims comprise: (a) Workmen's dues for the period of 24 months preceding the winding up order: ₹4 Crores; (b) Debt due to secured creditors having pari passu charge: ₹8 Crores; (c) Statutory taxes to Central Govt: ₹2 Crores. Under Section 326, how shall the realized proceeds of ₹10 Crores be distributed between workmen's dues and secured creditors?
options: Pari passu in proportion to their respective claims (Workmen get ₹3.33 Crores and Secured Creditors get ₹6.67 Crores) as overriding preferential payments, leaving zero for taxes.
Secured creditors are paid in full ₹8 Crores first, and remaining ₹2 Crores is paid to workmen.
Workmen dues of ₹4 Crores are paid in full first, and remaining ₹6 Crores is paid to secured creditors.
Statutory taxes of ₹2 Crores have first sovereign charge, and balance ₹8 Crores is shared equally.
questions.ref: Section 326(1) and 326(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 326(1) (Overriding Preferential Payments), workmen's dues and debts due to secured creditors to the extent of the workmen's portion shall be paid in priority to all other debts. If the assets are insufficient to meet them in full, they shall abate in equal proportions (pari passu). Ratio of workmen (₹4 Cr) : secured debt (₹8 Cr) = 1:2. Out of ₹10 Cr: Workmen receive ₹3.33 Cr and Secured Creditors receive ₹6.67 Cr.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 328 - Fraudulent Preference in Winding Up
questions.question: Omega Steels Ltd. made a transfer of property to an unsecured creditor, Mr. Bansal, to clear an antecedent loan on February 10, 2024. A petition for winding up was presented before NCLT on July 15, 2024, and winding up was ordered. The Company Liquidator applies under Section 328 to declare the transaction invalid. What is the look-back period for fraudulent preference under Section 328?
options: Any transfer made within 6 months before the presentation of the petition for winding up, if made with a view to give preference over other creditors.
Any transfer made within 1 year before the date of the winding up order.
Any transfer made within 2 years before insolvency initiation in case of related parties.
Any transaction made within 30 days prior to appointment of Provisional Liquidator.
questions.ref: Section 328 of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 328(1), where a company has given preference to any person who is a creditor or a surety or a guarantor, and the company does anything which has the effect of putting that person in a position better than other creditors in winding up, and such transaction took place within a period of six months before the presentation of a petition for winding up, it shall be deemed a fraudulent preference and invalid.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 420 & 421 - Appeal to NCLAT & Limitation Period
questions.question: The NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order against Crystal Glass Ltd. on May 10, 2024. The certified copy was received by Crystal Glass Ltd. on May 15, 2024. By what date must Crystal Glass Ltd. file an appeal before the NCLAT under Section 421(3), and what is the maximum condonable delay under the proviso?
options: File within 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order is made available (i.e. by June 29, 2024), with NCLAT having power to condone delay up to a further period not exceeding 45 days.
File within 30 days, with condonable delay of 15 days.
File within 60 days, with no power of condonation for delay.
File within 90 days from the date of pronouncement of the order.
questions.ref: Section 421(3) and Section 421(4) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 421(3), every appeal to NCLAT shall be filed within a period of 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order of the Tribunal is made available to the person aggrieved. Under Section 421(4), NCLAT may entertain an appeal after 45 days if satisfied there was sufficient cause, for a further period not exceeding 45 days.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 423 - Appeal to Supreme Court
questions.question: Any person aggrieved by any order of the Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) may file an appeal to the Supreme Court of India under Section 423 of the Companies Act, 2013. On what grounds can such appeal be filed, and within what timeframe?
options: On any question of law arising out of such order, within 60 days from the date of receipt of the order, with power to condone delay up to a further 60 days.
On any question of fact or law, within 30 days from the date of the order without any extension.
Only on violation of Fundamental Rights under Article 32 within 90 days.
Only on criminal contempt findings within 45 days.
questions.ref: Section 423 of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 423, any person aggrieved by any order of the Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court of India on any question of law arising out of such order within 60 days from the date of communication of the order. The Supreme Court may condone delay for a further period not exceeding 60 days.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 430 - Civil Court Bar of Jurisdiction
questions.question: A shareholder of Marvel Estates Ltd. files a civil suit in the City Civil Court seeking an injunction against the company from holding an Extraordinary General Meeting. The company argues that the Civil Court has no jurisdiction. Under Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013, what is the legal position?
options: No civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the NCLT or NCLAT is empowered to determine by or under this Act, and no injunction shall be granted by any court.
Civil courts have concurrent jurisdiction with NCLT in all shareholder dispute matters.
Civil courts can issue temporary injunctions up to 30 days before transferring the case to NCLT.
Section 430 applies only to winding up matters, leaving general meeting issues to High Courts.
questions.ref: Section 430 of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 430, no civil court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which the Tribunal or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to determine by or under this Act or any other law for the time being in force, and no injunction shall be granted by any court or other authority in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by this Act.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 273 - Powers of Tribunal on Petition
questions.question: Upon hearing a winding up petition under Section 273, the NCLT decides that an order of winding up would unfairly prejudice the petitioners, but that otherwise the facts justify winding up under the just and equitable ground. What order can the Tribunal pass under Section 273(1)?
options: The Tribunal may refuse to make an order of winding up and make any other interim or final order as it thinks fit, including orders under Chapter XVI (Oppression and Mismanagement).
The Tribunal is bound to pass an immediate winding up order regardless of unfair prejudice.
The Tribunal must refer the company compulsorily to the Central Government for nationalization.
The Tribunal must dismiss the petition with exemplary costs on the petitioners.
questions.ref: Section 273(1) and 273(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 273(2), where the petition is presented on the ground that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up, the Tribunal may refuse to make an order of winding up if it is of the opinion that some other remedy is available to the petitioners and that they are acting unreasonably in seeking to have the company wound up instead of pursuing that other remedy.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 277 - Intimation to Company Liquidator & ROC
questions.question: When a winding up order is passed by the Tribunal under Section 277, within what period must the Registrar of the Tribunal send intimation to the Company Liquidator and the Registrar of Companies?
options: Within a period not exceeding 7 days from the date of the order.
Within 24 hours of pronouncement.
Within 30 days of drawing up the certified decree.
Within 14 days from the date the order is signed by the President of NCLT.
questions.ref: Section 277(1) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 277(1), where the Tribunal makes an order for appointment of provisional liquidator or for winding up of a company, it shall, within a period not exceeding seven days from the date of passing of the order, cause intimation thereof to be sent to the Company Liquidator or provisional liquidator and to the Registrar of Companies.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Winding up, and the role of the NCLT and NCLAT
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 282 - Advisory Committee in Winding Up
questions.question: Under Section 282 of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal may direct that an Advisory Committee be constituted to advise the Company Liquidator. What is the maximum number of members in such an Advisory Committee?
options: Not more than 12 members being creditors and contributories of the company.
Exactly 5 members appointed by the Central Government.
Not more than 20 members representing employees and trade unions.
Any number decided by the Company Liquidator without ceiling.
questions.ref: Section 282(1) and 282(2) of the Companies Act, 2013
questions.explanation: Under Section 282(2), the Advisory Committee shall consist of not more than twelve members, being creditors and contributories of the company or persons holding general or special powers of attorney from creditors or contributories, in such proportions as the Tribunal may direct.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 7 - Designated Partners Requirement & Residency
questions.question: Apex Advisors LLP has 4 partners: Two are individuals (one an Indian citizen residing in Dubai who stayed in India for 80 days in FY 2023-24, and one a French national residing in India for 195 days in FY 2023-24), and two are body corporates. Who can be appointed as Designated Partners under Section 7 of the LLP Act, 2008 (as amended)?
options: Every LLP must have at least two designated partners who are individuals and at least one of them shall be a resident in India (stayed in India for not less than 120 days during the financial year); the French national qualifies as resident in India.
Only Indian citizens can be appointed as designated partners; foreign nationals are strictly barred.
Designated partners can only be corporate entities through their managing directors.
Residency requires a minimum stay of 182 days during the immediately preceding seven years.
questions.ref: Section 7(1) of LLP Act 2008 read with amended Explanation by LLP (Amendment) Act 2021
questions.explanation: Under Section 7(1), every LLP shall have at least two designated partners who are individuals and at least one of them shall be a resident in India. Under the LLP (Amendment) Act 2021, 'resident in India' means a person who has stayed in India for a period of not less than 120 days during the financial year. Citizenship is not required. Since the French national stayed 195 days (≥ 120 days), he satisfies the residency requirement.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 26 & 27 - Extent of Liability of LLP & Partner as Agent
questions.question: Mr. Dave, a partner in Zenith Logistics LLP, entered into a supply contract with a vendor for ₹25 Lakhs in the ordinary course of the business of the LLP. However, under the internal registered LLP Agreement, partners' borrowing/contracting power was capped at ₹10 Lakhs without prior approval of all partners. The vendor was unaware of this internal restriction. Is the LLP bound by the contract under Section 27?
options: Yes, the LLP is liable because a partner is an agent of the LLP, and the LLP is bound unless the partner had no authority and the third party knew that he had no authority or did not believe him to be a partner.
No, the contract is ultra vires the LLP Agreement and completely void ab initio.
Mr. Dave alone is personally liable for the full ₹25 Lakhs, and the LLP is completely exempt.
The contract is enforceable only up to ₹10 Lakhs, and balance ₹15 Lakhs is unenforceable.
questions.ref: Section 27(1) and 27(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 27(2), an LLP is liable for an obligation arising from a contract or otherwise in the course of its business. Under Section 27(1), an LLP is not bound by anything done by a partner in dealing with a person if: (a) the partner in fact has no authority to act for the LLP; AND (b) the person knows that he has no authority or does not know or believe him to be a partner. Since the vendor had no knowledge of the internal limit, the LLP is bound.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 30 - Unlimited Liability in Case of Fraud
questions.question: In Horizon Infotech LLP, partner Mr. Singhania, with the active knowledge and connivance of partner Mr. Gupta, carried on the business of the LLP with intent to defraud creditors by diverting funds to offshore personal accounts. Partner Ms. Roy had no knowledge and acted in good faith. What is the extent of liability under Section 30?
options: The liability of the LLP, Mr. Singhania, and Mr. Gupta shall be unlimited for all debts, while the liability of innocent partner Ms. Roy remains limited to her capital contribution.
All partners, including innocent partner Ms. Roy, incur unlimited personal liability jointly and severally.
The LLP cannot be held liable for criminal acts of its partners, making only Mr. Singhania personally liable.
Liability is limited to twice the capital contribution of each partner under the LLP Act.
questions.ref: Section 30(1) and 30(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 30(1), in the event of an act carried out by an LLP or any of its partners with intent to defraud creditors, the liability of the LLP and the partners who acted with intent to defraud shall be unlimited. However, under the proviso, where any partner has acted fraudulently, the LLP is liable to the same extent as the partner unless it is established that the act was done without the knowledge or authority of the LLP. An innocent partner without connivance retains limited liability.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 29 - Doctrine of Holding Out
questions.question: Mr. Mehta, who was never a partner in Quantum Tech LLP, represented himself as a partner on social media and at a commercial trade fair. Relying on this representation, a bank granted a loan of ₹40 Lakhs to the LLP. When the LLP defaulted, the bank sued Mr. Mehta. What is Mr. Mehta's liability under Section 29?
options: Mr. Mehta is liable by holding out to the bank who has on the faith of such representation given credit to the LLP.
Mr. Mehta incurs no liability because his name was not registered in the Ministry of Corporate Affairs LLP portal.
Mr. Mehta is only liable to pay a criminal fine of ₹10,000 to the Registrar.
The bank loses its claim because it failed to inspect the public register of partners.
questions.ref: Section 29(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 29(1) (Doctrine of Holding Out), anyone who by words spoken or written or by conduct represents himself, or knowingly permits himself to be represented to be a partner in an LLP, is liable to any person who has on the faith of any such representation given credit to the LLP, whether the person representing himself does or does not know that the representation has reached the creditor.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 34 - Maintenance of Books of Account & Solvency Statement
questions.question: Every LLP is required to prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency under Section 34(2). Within what period from the closure of each financial year must this statement be prepared and filed with the Registrar in Form 8?
options: Prepared within 6 months from the end of the financial year (by Sept 30) and filed with ROC within 30 days from the end of 6 months (i.e., by October 30).
Prepared and filed within 60 days from the end of the financial year (by May 30).
Prepared within 30 days and filed along with annual return by November 30.
Mandatory only for LLPs having capital contribution exceeding ₹1 Crore.
questions.ref: Section 34(2) and 34(3) read with Rule 24 of LLP Rules, 2009
questions.explanation: Under Section 34(2) read with Rule 24(4), every LLP shall prepare a Statement of Account and Solvency in Form 8 within a period of 6 months from the end of each financial year (by Sept 30) and file the same with the Registrar within 30 days from the end of 6 months of the financial year (by Oct 30).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 34(4) - Mandatory Audit of LLP Accounts Threshold
questions.question: Under Rule 24 of the Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009, an LLP is exempt from mandatory audit of its accounts if it satisfies which of the following criteria?
options: Its turnover does not exceed ₹40 Lakhs in any financial year AND its contribution does not exceed ₹25 Lakhs.
Its turnover does not exceed ₹1 Crore AND its contribution does not exceed ₹50 Lakhs.
Its turnover does not exceed ₹2 Crores regardless of contribution.
All LLPs are mandatorily required to be audited by a Chartered Accountant without exemption.
questions.ref: Rule 24(8) of the Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009
questions.explanation: Under Rule 24(8), an LLP whose turnover does not exceed, in any financial year, forty lakh rupees, or whose contribution does not exceed twenty-five lakh rupees, is not required to get its accounts audited. If either threshold is crossed (turnover > ₹40L or contribution > ₹25L), statutory audit by a CA in practice is mandatory.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 35 - Annual Return of LLP
questions.question: Under Section 35(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, every LLP shall file an annual return with the Registrar in Form 11 within what timeframe?
options: Within 60 days of closure of its financial year (i.e., by May 30).
Within 30 days of closure of its financial year (i.e., by April 30).
Within 180 days of closure of financial year (by September 30).
Simultaneously with the Statement of Account and Solvency on October 30.
questions.ref: Section 35(1) of the LLP Act, 2008 read with Rule 25 of LLP Rules, 2009
questions.explanation: Under Section 35(1) and Rule 25(1), every LLP shall file an annual return duly authenticated with the Registrar within 60 days of closure of its financial year in Form 11. For financial year ending March 31, the due date is May 30.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6 - Minimum Number of Partners & Sole Partner Liability
questions.question: Kestrel Solutions LLP had two partners, Mr. Roy and Mr. Sen. On August 1, 2023, Mr. Sen died in an accident. Mr. Roy continued carrying on the business of the LLP as the sole partner until March 31, 2024 (8 months) without admitting a new partner. Under Section 6(2), what is Mr. Roy's legal liability for debts contracted after February 1, 2024?
options: Mr. Roy is personally liable for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period after the expiry of 6 months (i.e., from February 1 onwards).
The LLP stands automatically dissolved on the date of death of Mr. Sen with zero liability for Mr. Roy.
Mr. Roy's liability remains strictly limited to his capital contribution under all circumstances.
Mr. Roy must pay a fine of ₹50,000 but incurs no personal liability for business debts.
questions.ref: Section 6(2) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 6(2), if at any time the number of partners of an LLP is reduced below two and the LLP carries on business for more than six months while the number is so reduced, the person who has the only partner of the LLP during the time that it so carries on business after those six months and has the knowledge of the fact that it is carrying on business with him alone, shall be liable personally for the obligations of the LLP incurred during that period.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 58 & Schedule III - Conversion of Private Company into LLP
questions.question: Starling Technologies Pvt. Ltd. wishes to convert into an LLP under Section 56 read with the Third Schedule. Which of the following conditions is mandatory for such conversion?
options: All the shareholders of the company must become partners of the LLP and no one else, and there must be no subsisting security interest in its assets at the date of application.
The conversion must be approved by the Reserve Bank of India.
The company must have paid dividends consistently for the past 3 financial years.
The company must have a minimum turnover of ₹5 Crores.
questions.ref: Section 56 read with Third Schedule (Paragraph 2 & 3) of LLP Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Paragraph 2 of the Third Schedule to the LLP Act 2008, a private company may convert into an LLP only if: (a) there is no security interest in its assets subsisting or in force at the time of application; and (b) the partners of the LLP to which it converts comprise all the shareholders of the company and no one else.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 64 - Circumstances in which LLP may be Wound Up by Tribunal
questions.question: Under Section 64 of the LLP Act, 2008, which of the following is NOT a ground on which the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) may wind up an LLP?
options: The LLP decides to distribute its profits in equal proportion rather than according to capital contribution.
The LLP is unable to pay its debts.
The number of partners of the LLP is reduced below two for a period of more than six months.
The LLP has made a default in filing with the Registrar the Statement of Account and Solvency or annual return for any five consecutive financial years.
questions.ref: Section 64 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 64, an LLP may be wound up by Tribunal if: (a) LLP decides it be wound up; (b) number of partners reduced below 2 for >6 months; (c) LLP unable to pay debts; (d) acted against sovereignty/security of India; (e) default in filing Statement of Account & Solvency or Annual Return for 5 consecutive years; or (f) just and equitable ground. Profit sharing ratios are determined by the agreement and is not a winding up ground.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 23 - LLP Agreement & First Schedule Fallback
questions.question: Three professionals incorporate an LLP without entering into a formal written LLP Agreement. In the absence of an agreement, how are the mutual rights and duties of the partners determined under Section 23(4)?
options: Determined by the default provisions set out in the First Schedule to the LLP Act, 2008 (including equal sharing of capital and profits, no remuneration, and equal rights in management).
Determined according to the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.
The LLP is deemed illegal and dissolved by ROC immediately.
The oldest partner has absolute power to dictate all management affairs.
questions.ref: Section 23(4) read with the First Schedule of the LLP Act, 2008
questions.explanation: Under Section 23(4), in the absence of agreement as to any matter, the mutual rights and duties of the partners and the mutual rights and duties of the LLP and the partners shall be determined by the provisions relating to that matter as set out in the First Schedule. Under First Schedule, all partners share equally in capital, profits, and management with no partner entitled to remuneration.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Minimum Threshold for Initiating CIRP
questions.question: Under Section 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC), what is the minimum default amount required to initiate Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against a corporate debtor as per the Central Government notification currently in force?
options: ₹1 Crore (One Crore Rupees).
₹1 Lakh (One Lakh Rupees).
₹10 Lakhs (Ten Lakh Rupees).
₹50 Lakhs (Fifty Lakh Rupees).
questions.ref: Section 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Notification S.O. 1205(E) dated 24.03.2020)
questions.explanation: Under Section 4 of the IBC, 2016, the default threshold for initiating CIRP was originally ₹1 Lakh. By notification dated March 24, 2020, the Central Government raised the minimum amount of default to ₹1 Crore in order to prevent MSMEs and other corporate entities from being pushed into insolvency for small defaults.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 7 - Initiation of CIRP by Financial Creditors
questions.question: A consortium of financial creditors comprising State Bank of India (holding 45% debt), Bank of Baroda (holding 30% debt), and Punjab National Bank (holding 25% debt) issues a recall notice to Krrish Infra Ltd. SBI desires to initiate CIRP under Section 7 of IBC, 2016. Can SBI file the application alone without joining the other consortium members?
options: Yes, a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors may file an application for initiating CIRP against a corporate debtor before the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT) when a default has occurred.
No, unanimous consent of all consortium members is mandatory under Section 7.
No, only lead bank holding at least 51% debt can file an application.
An application can only be filed after issuing a 90-day winding up notice.
questions.ref: Section 7(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 7(1) of the IBC, a financial creditor either by itself or jointly with other financial creditors, or any other person on behalf of the financial creditor, may file an application for initiating CIRP against a corporate debtor before the Adjudicating Authority when a default has occurred. Consortium consent is not a statutory prerequisite under Section 7.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 8 & 9 - Initiation of CIRP by Operational Creditor & Pre-existing Dispute
questions.question: Falcon Logistics delivers goods worth ₹1.2 Crores to Radiant Appliances Ltd. Due to quality defects, Radiant Appliances sent an email on March 5 disputing the invoice and debiting ₹40 Lakhs. Falcon Logistics issued a demand notice under Section 8 of IBC on April 10. Radiant replied on April 18 pointing out the pre-existing dispute regarding quality defects. Falcon Logistics files a Section 9 application before NCLT. How shall the NCLT decide?
options: The NCLT shall reject the application under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) because there is a genuine pre-existing dispute raised prior to the issuance of the demand notice.
The NCLT must admit the application because the invoice amount exceeds the ₹1 Crore threshold.
The NCLT must appoint an Interim Resolution Professional and ask the IRP to adjudicate the quality dispute.
The NCLT will direct Radiant Appliances to deposit 50% in court before examining the dispute.
questions.ref: Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC read with Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd. (SC)
questions.explanation: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) and the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Mobilox Innovations, if notice of a pre-existing dispute has been received by the operational creditor or there is a record of dispute in the information utility prior to the Section 8 demand notice, the Adjudicating Authority must reject the application. IBC is not a debt collection forum.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 14 - Moratorium Effect & Exemptions
questions.question: Upon admission of a CIRP application against Orbit Power Ltd., the NCLT declares a moratorium under Section 14. Which of the following actions is strictly prohibited during the moratorium period?
options: Institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor including execution of any judgment, decree or order in any court of law, tribunal, arbitration panel.
Supply of essential goods or services (such as electricity, water, telecommunications) to the corporate debtor.
Transactions by the corporate debtor in furtherance of its operations under the direction of the Resolution Professional.
Invocation of a performance bank guarantee given by a financial institution.
questions.ref: Section 14(1) and 14(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 14(1)(a), the declaration of moratorium strictly prohibits the institution of suits or continuation of pending suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor. Conversely, essential goods/services cannot be terminated (Sec 14(2)) and performance bank guarantees are exempt from moratorium under the amended Section 14(3).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 21 & 24 - Committee of Creditors (CoC) Composition & Voting Share
questions.question: In the CIRP of Titan Steel Ltd., the Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises Financial Creditor A (voting share 50%), Financial Creditor B (voting share 20%), and Financial Creditor C (a related party of the corporate debtor having 30% financial debt). What is the voting right of Financial Creditor C in the CoC meetings under Section 21(2)?
options: Financial Creditor C has zero right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the Committee of Creditors, and the remaining creditors' voting shares will be normalized to 100%.
Financial Creditor C can participate and vote on ordinary matters but not on resolution plan approval.
Financial Creditor C has equal voting rights provided NCLT grants permission.
Financial Creditor C votes with 50% discount on its voting power.
questions.ref: First proviso to Section 21(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under the first proviso to Section 21(2), a financial creditor or the authorised representative of the financial creditor, if it is a related party of the corporate debtor, shall not have any right of representation, participation or voting in a meeting of the Committee of Creditors. Its debt is excluded when computing total voting share.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 30(4) - CoC Voting Threshold for Resolution Plan
questions.question: A resolution plan submitted by Star Mining Ltd. in respect of a corporate debtor is put to vote in the CoC meeting. Creditors holding 64% voting share vote in favor of the plan, 20% vote against, and 16% abstain. What is the fate of the resolution plan under Section 30(4)?
options: The resolution plan is rejected because approval of a resolution plan mandatorily requires not less than 66% of voting share of the financial creditors.
The resolution plan is approved because 64% out of participating creditors (64 / 84 = 76.19%) exceeds the 66% threshold.
The plan is approved because simple majority (51%) is sufficient under the amended rules.
The Resolution Professional can exercise a casting vote to approve the plan.
questions.ref: Section 30(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 30(4), the Committee of Creditors may approve a resolution plan by a vote of not less than sixty-six percent (66%) of voting share of the financial creditors. The percentage is calculated based on the total voting share of the CoC, not merely those present and voting. Since 64% < 66%, the resolution plan stands rejected.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 29A - Persons Ineligible to be Resolution Applicants
questions.question: Mr. Singhal submitted a resolution plan for an insolvent textile company. An investigation reveals that Mr. Singhal was a promoter of an entity whose account was classified as a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) by a commercial bank 18 months prior to the CIRP commencement date, and such default continues. Is Mr. Singhal eligible to submit a resolution plan under Section 29A(c)?
options: No, he is disqualified under Section 29A(c) as his account has been classified as NPA for a period of at least one year prior to the commencement of CIRP, unless he pays all overdue amounts with interest before submitting the plan.
Yes, he is fully eligible provided he pays a processing deposit of ₹50 Lakhs to the CoC.
Yes, the NPA disqualification applies only to willful defaulters, not ordinary NPA promoters.
Disqualification under Section 29A applies only to foreign citizens.
questions.ref: Section 29A(c) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 29A(c), a person is ineligible to submit a resolution plan if at the time of submission of the plan has an account, or an account of a corporate debtor under his management or control, classified as NPA for a period of at least one year prior to the date of commencement of CIRP, and such person has failed to pay in full all overdue amounts with interest thereon and other charges before submission of the plan.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53 - Distribution of Assets (Waterfall Mechanism)
questions.question: In the liquidation of Galaxy Electronics Ltd., the liquidator realizes ₹100 Crores. The claims include: (a) CIRP costs and liquidation costs: ₹5 Crores; (b) Workmen dues (past 24 months) and secured debts of creditors who relinquished security: ₹40 Crores; (c) Wages of employees other than workmen (past 12 months): ₹10 Crores; (d) Central Government taxes: ₹15 Crores. Under Section 53, who gets paid first after meeting the insolvency resolution process costs?
options: Workmen's dues for 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date and debts owed to a secured creditor in the event such secured creditor has relinquished security to the liquidation estate, ranking equally.
Central Government taxes under the sovereign priority rule.
Unsecured financial creditors.
Wages and salaries of non-workmen employees for 12 months.
questions.ref: Section 53(1)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 53(1) (Waterfall Mechanism): (a) CIRP costs and liquidation costs are paid first in full; (b) Next, workmen's dues for the period of 24 months preceding liquidation commencement date AND debts owed to a secured creditor who has relinquished security under Section 52 rank equally (pari passu); (c) Wages and unpaid dues to employees other than workmen for 12 months; (d) Unsecured financial debts; (e) Government dues and remaining secured debts.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 12 - Time-limit for Completion of CIRP
questions.question: Under Section 12 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, what is the statutory period for completing the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), including any extension and litigation period?
options: Mandatorily completed within 180 days, extendable once by the Adjudicating Authority by up to 90 days upon CoC approval (66%), with overall completion mandatorily within 330 days from insolvency commencement date including legal proceedings.
Completed within 90 days, extendable by another 90 days without any outer cap.
Completed within 365 days with no discretion for NCLT to extend.
Completed within 60 days for all public companies.
questions.ref: Section 12(1), 12(2) and 12(3) second proviso of the IBC, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 12(1), the CIRP shall be completed within a period of 180 days. Under Section 12(3), NCLT may extend this period by a maximum of 90 days if instructed by CoC with 66% majority. Under the second proviso to Section 12(3), the CIRP shall mandatorily be completed within a period of 330 days from the insolvency commencement date, including any extension and time taken in legal proceedings.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 43 - Preferential Transactions and Relevant Time
questions.question: During CIRP, the Resolution Professional finds that the corporate debtor transferred an unencumbered commercial property to an unsecured financial creditor (who is a non-related party) to extinguish a 3-year-old loan, 8 months prior to the insolvency commencement date. Under Section 43, what is the relevant 'look-back period' for avoiding preferential transactions for non-related parties?
options: A period of one year preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of six months preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of two years preceding the insolvency commencement date.
A period of three years preceding the admission order.
questions.ref: Section 43(4)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 43(4), a preference shall be deemed to be given at a relevant time if: (a) it is given to a related party during the period of two years preceding the insolvency commencement date; OR (b) it is given to a person other than a related party during the period of one year preceding the insolvency commencement date. Since 8 months < 1 year, the transaction is avoidable as a preference.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 45 - Undervalued Transactions
questions.question: The corporate debtor gifted machinery valued at ₹2 Crores to a relative of the promoter for a consideration of ₹10 Lakhs, 18 months prior to the insolvency commencement date. Can the Resolution Professional apply to the Adjudicating Authority to declare this transaction void under Section 45?
options: Yes, because for transactions with a related party, the look-back period for undervalued transactions under Section 46(1) is two years preceding the insolvency commencement date.
No, the look-back period for undervalued transactions is strictly capped at one year for all parties.
No, because consideration was paid, and any positive consideration precludes undervaluation.
Only the Central Government can file an avoidance application under Section 45.
questions.ref: Section 45(1) and Section 46(1)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 45, where a transaction is undervalued, the RP may make an application to NCLT. Under Section 46(1), the relevant period is: (a) one year preceding insolvency commencement date for non-related persons; and (b) two years preceding insolvency commencement date where the transaction was with a related party. Since 18 months < 2 years, it is an avoidable undervalued transaction.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 66 - Fraudulent Trading or Wrongful Trading
questions.question: During CIRP, forensic audit reveals that the directors of the corporate debtor continued to accept customer advance payments knowing fully well that the company had no manufacturing capability and insolvency was inevitable. What liability can the NCLT impose under Section 66(2)?
options: The NCLT may direct that such director shall be personally liable to make such contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor as it thinks fit, because before the insolvency commencement date he knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding CIRP.
The NCLT can only disqualify the directors from future directorships under Section 164 of Companies Act.
The directors incur criminal liability only with no financial contribution to corporate assets.
The liability is limited to the unpaid share capital on their equity shares.
questions.ref: Section 66(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
questions.explanation: Under Section 66(2) (Wrongful Trading), on an application made by the RP, the Adjudicating Authority may direct that a director or partner shall be liable to make such contribution to the assets of the corporate debtor as it may deem fit, if before the insolvency commencement date, such person knew or ought to have known that there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding commencement of CIRP and failed to exercise due diligence.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 11B - Power of SEBI to Issue Directions & Impound Proceeds
questions.question: Under Section 11B of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Act, 1992, which of the following measures can SEBI direct against an intermediary or market participant in the interests of investors or orderly market development?
options: Suspend the trading of any security in a recognized stock exchange, restrain persons from accessing the securities market, and direct impounding and retention of all proceeds or securities involved in the violation.
Direct the compulsory dissolution of the corporate entity without reference to NCLT.
Cancel the Indian passport of the company's directors.
Order military custody of the company's premises.
questions.ref: Section 11(4) and Section 11B of the SEBI Act, 1992
questions.explanation: Under Section 11(4) and 11B, SEBI has comprehensive powers to issue directions including: (a) suspending trading of any security; (b) restraining persons from accessing the securities market; (c) impounding and retaining proceeds; and (d) directing attachment of bank accounts for up to 90 days.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15G - Penalty for Insider Trading
questions.question: An insider of a listed entity trades in the securities of the company on the basis of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) and earns unlawful profits of ₹8 Crores. Under Section 15G of the SEBI Act, 1992, what is the maximum monetary penalty that can be imposed by the Adjudicating Officer?
options: A penalty which shall not be less than ₹10 Lakhs, but which may extend to ₹25 Crores or three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading, whichever is higher (i.e. up to ₹25 Crores or ₹24 Crores -> max ₹25 Crores).
Fixed penalty of ₹1 Crore only.
A penalty strictly capped at double the investment value.
Fine up to ₹50 Lakhs with mandatory 7 years imprisonment.
questions.ref: Section 15G of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
questions.explanation: Under Section 15G, if any insider deals in securities on the basis of UPSI or communicates UPSI, he shall be liable to a penalty which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees, but which may extend to twenty-five crore rupees or three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading, whichever is higher.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15T & 15Z - Appeal to SAT and Supreme Court
questions.question: An order imposing a monetary penalty is passed by the Adjudicating Officer of SEBI on May 2. By what date must the aggrieved entity file an appeal before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) under Section 15T, and within what period may an appeal against SAT order be filed to the Supreme Court under Section 15Z?
options: Appeal to SAT within 45 days from the date of receipt of copy of order; Appeal against SAT order to Supreme Court on question of law within 60 days from communication of order.
Appeal to SAT within 30 days; Appeal to Supreme Court within 30 days.
Appeal to SAT within 60 days; Appeal to Supreme Court within 90 days.
Appeal to SAT within 15 days; Appeal to High Court within 30 days.
questions.ref: Section 15T(3) and Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, 1992
questions.explanation: Under Section 15T(3), every appeal to the Securities Appellate Tribunal shall be filed within a period of 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order is received. Under Section 15Z, any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Securities Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the Supreme Court for any question of law arising out of such order within 60 days from the date of communication.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 17 - Board Composition & Independent Directors
questions.question: Under Regulation 17(1) of SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, if the Chairperson of the Board of Directors of a listed entity is a non-executive director and is a promoter or related to any promoter, what proportion of the Board must comprise Independent Directors?
options: At least half (50%) of the Board of Directors shall consist of Independent Directors.
At least one-third (33.33%) of the Board of Directors.
At least two-thirds (66.67%) of the Board of Directors.
Only 2 independent directors are required regardless of promoter relation.
questions.ref: Regulation 17(1)(b) proviso of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 17(1)(b), where the chairperson of the board of directors is a non-executive director, at least one-third of the board of directors shall comprise of independent directors. However, under the proviso, where the non-executive chairperson is a promoter of the listed entity or is related to any promoter or person occupying management positions, at least half (50%) of the board of directors shall consist of independent directors.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 18 - Audit Committee Composition & Quorum
questions.question: Under Regulation 18 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, which of the following requirements regarding the Audit Committee of a listed entity is MANDATORY?
options: The Audit Committee shall have minimum 3 directors as members, at least two-thirds of the members shall be independent directors, and the Chairperson shall be an independent director who shall be present at AGM.
All members of the Audit Committee must be executive directors with accounting degrees.
Audit Committee quorum is one director personally present.
Audit Committee is required to meet only once every financial year.
questions.ref: Regulation 18(1) and 18(2) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 18(1), the Audit Committee must have minimum 3 directors, at least two-thirds of the members shall be independent directors (for listed entities with SR equity shares, all members must be independent), and the Chairperson shall be an independent director present at the AGM. Quorum is two members or one-third, whichever is greater, with at least two independent directors.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 23 - Material Related Party Transactions (RPT)
questions.question: Under Regulation 23 of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, a transaction with a related party shall be considered 'material' if the transaction(s) to be entered into individually or taken together with previous transactions during a financial year exceeds which threshold?
options: ₹1,000 Crore OR 10% of the annual consolidated turnover of the listed entity as per the last audited financial statements, whichever is lower.
₹100 Crore or 5% of turnover, whichever is higher.
10% of net worth of the holding company exclusively.
₹500 Crore regardless of consolidated turnover.
questions.ref: Regulation 23(1) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 (as amended)
questions.explanation: Under amended Regulation 23(1), a transaction with a related party shall be considered material if the transaction(s) to be entered into individually or taken together with previous transactions during a financial year, exceeds ₹1,000 Crore or 10% of the annual consolidated turnover of the listed entity as per the last audited financial statements, whichever is lower. Prior shareholder approval by ordinary resolution is required.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (LODR) Reg 30 - Disclosure of Material Events to Stock Exchanges
questions.question: A listed pharmaceutical company discovers an unexpected fire accident causing severe damage of ₹60 Crores to its active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing unit. Under Regulation 30 read with Schedule III of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, within what timeframe must the listed entity disclose this material event to stock exchanges?
options: As soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours from the occurrence of the event (or 12 hours if originating from within the company).
Within 7 days of completion of the insurance surveyor's assessment.
At the immediate next quarterly financial results announcement.
Within 48 hours of Board approval of the restoration plan.
questions.ref: Regulation 30(6) of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015 (as amended in 2023)
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 30(6) as amended, the listed entity shall disclose to the stock exchange(s) all material events as soon as reasonably possible and in any case not later than: (i) 30 minutes from closure of Board meeting for decisions; (ii) 12 hours from occurrence if originating from within; (iii) 24 hours from occurrence if not originating from within.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (PIT) Reg 2(1)(n) - Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)
questions.question: Under Regulation 2(1)(n) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, which of the following is explicitly deemed to be Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI)?
options: Financial results, dividends, change in capital structure, mergers, de-mergers, acquisitions, delistings, disposals and expansion of business, and changes in Key Managerial Personnel.
Routine quarterly sales volume disclosures published on company website.
Public press releases announcing award of industry excellence trophies.
Employee retirement notices below managerial cadre.
questions.ref: Regulation 2(1)(n) of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 2(1)(n), 'unpublished price sensitive information' means any information, relating to a company or its securities, directly or indirectly, that is not generally available which upon becoming generally available is likely to materially affect the price of securities, including: financial results, dividends, change in capital structure, M&A/restructuring, and changes in KMP.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (PIT) Reg 9 - Trading Window Closure Period
questions.question: Under Clause 4 of Schedule B read with Regulation 9 of SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015, trading window restrictions shall mandatorily be applied by listed entities from which date until when?
options: From the end of every quarter till 48 hours after the declaration of financial results.
From 7 days before the Board meeting till 24 hours after results declaration.
Only on the exact day of the Board meeting approving financial statements.
From the beginning of the financial year till the Annual General Meeting.
questions.ref: Clause 4 of Schedule B of SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
questions.explanation: Under Clause 4 of Schedule B (Minimum Standards for Code of Conduct), trading restriction period shall be made applicable from the end of every quarter till 48 hours after the declaration of financial results. Designated persons and their immediate relatives are prohibited from trading during this window closure.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (SAST) Reg 3 - Substantial Acquisition Threshold (Trigger Limit)
questions.question: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011 (SAST), what is the threshold of voting rights that triggers the mandatory obligation to make a public announcement of an open offer to acquire shares from public shareholders?
options: Acquiring shares or voting rights which taken together with existing holdings entitle the acquirer and PACs to exercise 25% or more of voting rights in the target company.
Acquiring 15% or more of voting rights.
Acquiring 51% or more of paid-up equity share capital.
Acquiring any voting rights exceeding 5% in a single financial year.
questions.ref: Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, no acquirer shall acquire shares or voting rights in a target company which taken together with shares or voting rights held by him and by persons acting in concert (PAC) with him in such target company, entitle them to exercise twenty-five per cent (25%) or more of the voting rights, unless the acquirer makes a public announcement of an open offer.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: SEBI Act and key SEBI regulations
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] SEBI (SAST) Reg 3(2) - Creeping Acquisition Limit
