questions.question: An acquirer holds 38% voting rights in an equity listed company. During FY 2024-25, the acquirer desires to purchase additional shares from the open market without triggering a mandatory open offer. What is the maximum percentage of voting rights the acquirer can acquire under the 'creeping acquisition' provision of Regulation 3(2)?
options: Up to 5% of voting rights in that financial year, provided the acquisition does not result in total holding exceeding maximum permissible non-public shareholding (75%).
Up to 10% of voting rights in any financial year.
Up to 2% of voting rights every quarter.
Zero additional shares can be acquired without an open offer once holding exceeds 25%.
questions.ref: Regulation 3(2) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 3(2), an acquirer who holds 25% or more but less than maximum permissible non-public shareholding (75%) may acquire additional shares or voting rights entitling him to exercise more than 5% of voting rights in any financial year only by making an open offer. Therefore, acquisitions up to 5% in a financial year (creeping acquisition) are permitted without an open offer.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 2(v) - Residential Status under FEMA
questions.question: Mr. Rohan, an Indian citizen, resided in India for 210 days during FY 2022-23. On May 10, 2023, he went to London to take up an employment contract for a duration of 3 years. What is Mr. Rohan's residential status under Section 2(v) of FEMA, 1999 for FY 2023-24?
options: Person Resident Outside India (PROI) with effect from May 10, 2023, because he went outside India for taking up employment outside India.
Person Resident in India (PRII) for the entire FY 2023-24 because his stay in India in FY 2022-23 exceeded 182 days.
Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident as defined under the Income-tax Act, 1961.
Dual resident entitled to relief under double tax avoidance agreements.
questions.ref: Section 2(v)(i)(A) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
questions.explanation: Under Section 2(v)(i), 'person resident in India' means a person residing in India for more than 182 days during the course of the preceding financial year, but DOES NOT INCLUDE a person who has gone out of India or who stays outside India for or on taking up employment outside India (Clause A). Since Rohan went abroad for employment, he becomes a Person Resident Outside India (PROI) from the date of departure.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 5 & FEM (CAT) Rules - Prohibited Current Account Transactions
questions.question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, which of the following current account transactions is completely PROHIBITED under Schedule I?
options: Remittance out of lottery winnings, racing/riding income, purchase of lottery tickets, football pools, and sweepstakes.
Remittance for cultural tours.
Remittance for hiring transponders for TV channels.
Remittance of commission on exports under Rupee State Credit Route.
questions.ref: Schedule I of FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000 read with Section 5
questions.explanation: Under Schedule I of FEM (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000, remittance out of lottery winnings, remittance of income from racing/riding or any other hobby, remittance for purchase of lottery tickets, banned/proscribed magazines, football pools, sweepstakes, etc., are completely prohibited.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Schedule III & LRS - Liberalised Remittance Scheme Ceiling
questions.question: Mr. Kapoor, an individual resident in India, intends to remit foreign exchange abroad for his son's overseas education and his family holiday. Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) of RBI read with Schedule III of FEM (CAT) Rules, what is the annual permissible ceiling for all permissible current and capital account transactions per financial year?
options: Up to USD 2,50,000 (Two Hundred Fifty Thousand US Dollars) or its equivalent per financial year (April-March) without prior RBI approval.
Up to USD 1,00,000 per financial year.
Up to USD 5,00,000 per calendar year.
Unlimited remittances provided TCS at 20% is collected.
questions.ref: Schedule III of FEM (CAT) Rules, 2000 read with RBI A.P. (DIR Series) Circulars on LRS
questions.explanation: Under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), resident individuals are freely permitted to remit up to USD 2,50,000 per financial year (April-March) for any permissible current or capital account transactions or a combination of both without prior approval of RBI. Any remittance exceeding USD 2,50,000 requires prior approval of the Reserve Bank.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6 - Permissible Capital Account Transactions
questions.question: Which of the following is explicitly classified as a 'Capital Account Transaction' under Section 2(e) read with Section 6 of FEMA, 1999?
options: Investment in foreign securities by a resident Indian, raising of foreign currency loans (ECBs), and transfer of immovable property outside India by a person resident in India.
Payment due as interest on loans and as net income from investments.
Remittance for living expenses of parents residing abroad.
Payment due in connection with foreign trade and short-term banking credit facilities.
questions.ref: Section 2(e) and Section 6(3) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
questions.explanation: Under Section 2(e), 'capital account transaction' means a transaction which alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India or assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India. Foreign security investments, foreign loans (ECBs), and overseas immovable property transfers alter such balance sheets and are capital account transactions.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] FDI Policy - Prohibited Sectors for Foreign Direct Investment
questions.question: Under the Consolidated Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) Policy and Non-Debt Instruments (NDI) Rules, 2019, in which of the following sectors is Foreign Direct Investment completely PROHIBITED?
options: Lottery business, gambling and betting, chit funds, Nidhi company, trading in Transferable Development Rights (TDRs), Real Estate Business or construction of farm houses, manufacturing of cigars, cheroots, cigarillos and cigarettes of tobacco.
Single-brand product retail trading.
Civil aviation and non-scheduled air transport services.
Pharmaceuticals (Greenfield manufacturing).
questions.ref: Rule 15 read with Schedule I of FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
questions.explanation: FDI is strictly prohibited in: (a) Lottery business including government/private lottery, online lotteries; (b) Gambling and betting including casinos; (c) Chit funds; (d) Nidhi company; (e) Trading in TDRs; (f) Real Estate Business (excluding township/construction development); (g) Manufacturing of cigars/cigarettes; (h) Sectors not open to private investment (Atomic energy & Railway operations).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Land Border FDI Restrictions (Press Note 3 / Rule 6 Proviso)
questions.question: Under the proviso to Rule 6 of the FEM (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 (reflecting Press Note 3 of 2020), an entity of a country which shares a land border with India can invest in Indian companies only under which route?
options: Only under the Government Approval Route, regardless of the sector or percentage of foreign holding.
Under 100% Automatic Route provided it is in technology manufacturing.
Under Automatic Route up to 49% and Government Route beyond 49%.
Investments from land-border countries are permanently barred.
questions.ref: Proviso to Rule 6(a) of Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Rule 6(a), an entity of a country which shares land border with India or where the beneficial owner of an investment into India is situated in or is a citizen of any such country, can invest only under the Government approval route. Automatic route is completely unavailable.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) Rules 2022 - Financial Commitment Limit
questions.question: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, what is the maximum permissible limit of total financial commitment in all foreign entities by an Indian entity under the Automatic Route?
options: Up to 400% (four hundred percent) of the net worth of the Indian entity as per the last audited balance sheet, or USD 1 Billion per financial year, whichever is less.
Up to 100% of the net worth of the Indian entity.
Up to 200% of paid-up share capital exclusively.
Capped at USD 100 Million per project.
questions.ref: Rule 13(1) and Schedule I of FEM (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022
questions.explanation: Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, the total financial commitment made by an Indian entity in all foreign entities shall not exceed 400% of its net worth as per the last audited balance sheet, or as prescribed by RBI from time to time under the automatic route.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) - Framework & Minimum Maturity
questions.question: Under the Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) issued by the Reserve Bank of India, what is the Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) for foreign currency denominated ECBs raised up to USD 750 Million per financial year under the Automatic Route for general corporate purposes?
options: Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) of 5 years (or 3 years for eligible manufacturing sector companies).
MAMP of 1 year.
MAMP of 10 years without exception.
No maturity requirement if interest is paid semi-annually.
questions.ref: RBI Master Direction No. 5/2018-19 on External Commercial Borrowings (ECB Framework)
questions.explanation: Under the RBI ECB framework, the Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) for general corporate / working capital purposes is 5 years. For specific manufacturing companies, it can be 3 years for borrowings up to USD 50 Million.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 13 - Penalties for Contravention of FEMA
questions.question: If any person contravenes any provision of FEMA, 1999 or any rule, regulation, direction or order issued thereunder, what is the monetary penalty leviable under Section 13(1) where the amount involved is quantifiable?
options: Up to thrice (3 times) the sum involved in such contravention, and where the amount is not quantifiable, up to ₹2 Lakhs, and for continuing contravention a further penalty up to ₹5,000 per day.
Fixed penalty equal to 100% of the transaction amount.
Imprisonment for 7 years without option of monetary penalty.
A penalty up to ₹10 Lakhs strictly.
questions.ref: Section 13(1) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999
questions.explanation: Under Section 13(1), if any person contravenes any provision of this Act, or any rule, regulation, notification, direction or order, he shall be liable to a penalty up to thrice the sum involved in such contravention where the amount is quantifiable, or up to two lakh rupees where the amount is not quantifiable, and where such contravention is a continuing one, further penalty which may extend to five thousand rupees for every day after the first day.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 15 - Compounding of Contraventions
questions.question: Under Section 15 of FEMA, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2000, which of the following contraventions CANNOT be compounded by the Reserve Bank of India?
options: A contravention where a similar contravention committed by the person was compounded within a period of three years from the date of the present contravention, or contraventions involving serious money laundering/hawala angles.
Failure to file Advance Reporting Form within 30 days of receiving inward remittance.
Delay in filing Form FC-GPR beyond 30 days of share allotment.
Borrowing ECB exceeding the prescribed all-in-cost ceiling.
questions.ref: Section 15(1) proviso of FEMA, 1999 and Rule 4 of Compounding Proceedings Rules, 2000
questions.explanation: Under the proviso to Section 15(1), where a contravention has been compounded, no further compounding of that contravention shall be done within a period of 3 years from the date on which that contravention was compounded. Any second contravention committed within 3 years must go to regular adjudication. Also, contraventions involving serious PMLA violations cannot be compounded by RBI.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Holding of Foreign Exchange by Resident Indian
questions.question: Under Section 4 of FEMA, 1999 read with Foreign Exchange Management (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2015, what is the maximum amount of foreign currency notes/coins an individual resident in India can retain in cash for personal use?
options: Up to USD 2,000 (or its equivalent in foreign currency notes/coins) without opening an RFC(D) account.
Up to USD 10,000 in cash notes.
Zero cash retention; all foreign currency must be surrendered within 24 hours of landing in India.
Up to USD 50,000 provided it was received as a gift.
questions.ref: Regulation 3 of FEM (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, 2015
questions.explanation: Under Regulation 3 of FEM (Realisation, Repatriation and Surrender of Foreign Exchange) Regulations, a person resident in India is permitted to retain foreign currency notes, bank notes and foreign currency travellers' cheques exceeding not more than USD 2,000 or its equivalent in aggregate, provided they were acquired while on a visit abroad or from an authorized person for business travel.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 3(3) - Cartels & Horizontal Anti-Competitive Agreements
questions.question: Four leading cement manufacturers in western India enter into an informal unwritten understanding on WhatsApp to fix the ex-factory dispatch price of OPC 53 grade cement and collectively limit monthly production volumes to create artificial scarcity. Under Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002, what presumption applies to such horizontal agreements?
options: Such agreement shall be presumed to have an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC), shifting the burden of proof onto the cement manufacturers to rebut the presumption.
The agreement is presumed legal unless the Competition Commission of India proves actual consumer loss in rupees.
Informal unwritten understandings cannot be treated as an agreement under Section 2(b).
Cartels are exempt from the Competition Act if cement is notified as an essential commodity.
questions.ref: Section 3(3) of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 3(3), any agreement entered into between enterprises or associations of enterprises engaged in identical or similar trade of goods or provision of services (horizontal agreements/cartels), which: (a) determines purchase or sale prices; (b) limits or controls production, supply, markets, technical development; (c) shares the market; or (d) results in bid rigging, shall be PRESUMED to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 3(4) - Vertical Agreements & Rule of Reason
questions.question: A manufacturer of high-end sports cars requires all authorized dealers to sign a contract stipulating that dealers cannot sell cars below the minimum retail price prescribed by the manufacturer (Resale Price Maintenance) and cannot sell spare parts of competing brands (Exclusive Supply Agreement). How does the Competition Commission of India evaluate vertical agreements under Section 3(4)?
options: Under the 'Rule of Reason' test, assessing whether the agreement causes or is likely to cause an Appreciable Adverse Effect on Competition (AAEC) under the factors listed in Section 19(3).
Vertical agreements are per se illegal with strict statutory presumption of AAEC.
All dealership contracts are unconditionally valid under the freedom of contract principle.
CCI has no jurisdiction over vertical agreements between manufacturers and distributors.
questions.ref: Section 3(4) read with Section 19(3) of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Unlike horizontal agreements under Section 3(3) which carry a statutory presumption of AAEC, vertical agreements under Section 3(4) (such as tie-in arrangement, exclusive supply agreement, exclusive distribution agreement, refusal to deal, and resale price maintenance) are evaluated under the 'Rule of Reason' to determine if they cause or are likely to cause an AAEC under Section 19(3).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 4 - Abuse of Dominant Position & Predatory Pricing
questions.question: Mega Telecom Ltd. holds a 68% market share in the relevant market for high-speed fiber internet services in Metro Zone. In order to drive out two newly launched regional competitors, Mega Telecom reduces its subscription price to ₹99 per month, which is far below its Average Variable Cost (AVC), while utilizing huge capital reserves. What specific abuse of dominant position does this constitute under Section 4?
options: Predatory Pricing under Section 4(2)(a)(ii) read with Explanation (b), being the sale of services at a price below cost with a view to reduce competition or eliminate competitors.
Fair promotional marketing permissible under consumer welfare schemes.
Legitimate price discrimination permitted under Section 4(2)(c).
An anti-competitive combination under Section 5.
questions.ref: Section 4(2)(a)(ii) read with Explanation (b) of Section 4 of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 4(2)(a)(ii), there is an abuse of dominant position if an enterprise directly or indirectly imposes unfair or discriminatory price in purchase or sale of goods or service, including predatory price. Under Explanation (b), 'predatory price' means the sale of goods or provision of services at a price below the cost, as determined by regulations, with a view to reduce competition or eliminate competitors.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 5 & 6 - Regulation of Combinations (Thresholds)
questions.question: Under Section 5 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as revised and amended), which of the following transactions constitutes a 'Combination' mandating prior approval of the Competition Commission of India (CCI) under Section 6?
options: Any acquisition, merger or amalgamation where the enterprise or group exceeds the prescribed statutory asset or turnover thresholds in India or abroad, OR where the Deal Value Threshold (DVT) exceeds ₹2,000 Crores and the target enterprise has substantial business operations in India.
Any merger where both companies are incorporated in the same State regardless of size.
Only mergers involving foreign multinational corporations with market share > 90%.
Any acquisition where payment is made in cash exceeding ₹100 Crores.
questions.ref: Section 5 and Section 6 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
questions.explanation: Under Section 5 as amended by the Competition (Amendment) Act 2023, a combination includes: (a) asset and turnover threshold criteria (individual enterprise or group); and (b) Deal Value Threshold (DVT), where the value of any transaction in connection with acquisition, merger or amalgamation exceeds ₹2,000 Crores and the enterprise has substantial business operations in India. Section 6 mandates prior notification to CCI.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 6(2A) - Timeline for CCI Approval of Combinations
questions.question: Under the amended Section 6(2A) of the Competition Act, 2002, what is the maximum statutory timeline within which the CCI must pass an order approving or rejecting a combination, failing which the combination shall be deemed to have been approved?
options: Within a period of 150 days (reduced from 210 days by the 2023 Amendment) from the date of filing notice.
Within 30 working days without any extension.
Within 365 days from the date of publishing public notice.
Within 60 days of hearing objections from third parties.
questions.ref: Section 6(2A) of the Competition Act, 2002 (amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
questions.explanation: Under the Competition (Amendment) Act 2023, Section 6(2A) reduced the outer timeline for CCI to form a prima facie opinion and pass an order on a combination from 210 days to 150 days (and prima facie opinion timeline reduced to 30 days). If CCI fails to pass an order within 150 days, the combination is deemed to have been approved.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 27 - Orders and Penalties for Cartels
questions.question: Where the CCI finds that 5 tyre manufacturing companies formed a price-fixing cartel in contravention of Section 3, what is the maximum penalty the CCI can impose on each cartel member under Section 27(b)?
options: Up to three times of its profit for each year of the continuance of such agreement, OR ten per cent of its turnover for each year of the continuance of such agreement, whichever is higher (and now including global turnover).
Fixed penalty of ₹5 Crores on each company.
Penalties are restricted to 1% of domestic sales.
Compulsory confiscation of all factory machinery without monetary penalty.
questions.ref: Section 27(b) proviso of the Competition Act, 2002 (amended by Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023)
questions.explanation: Under Section 27(b) proviso, in case of a cartel, the Commission may impose upon each producer, seller, distributor, trader or service provider included in that cartel, a penalty of up to three times of its profit for each year of the continuance of such agreement or ten per cent of its turnover for each year of the continuance of such agreement, whichever is higher. The 2023 Amendment clarified that turnover includes global turnover derived from all products and services.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 46 - Lesser Penalty Regulations (Leniency Programme)
questions.question: Alpha Glass Ltd., a member of a covert glass cartel, approaches the CCI and makes full, vital, and true disclosure about the existence, operations, and pricing formulas of the cartel before the Director General (DG) submits an investigation report. What benefit can Alpha Glass Ltd. receive under Section 46?
options: The Commission may grant up to 100% reduction in penalty to the first applicant who makes a vital disclosure enabling the Commission to form a prima facie opinion or establish the existence of the cartel.
Complete immunity from paying taxes to the Central Government.
A cash reward of ₹50 Lakhs from the Prime Minister's Relief Fund.
The leniency provisions apply only to non-corporate partnership firms.
questions.ref: Section 46 of the Competition Act, 2002 read with CCI (Lesser Penalty) Regulations, 2024
questions.explanation: Under Section 46 read with the Lesser Penalty Regulations, the CCI may grant up to 100% reduction in penalty to the first applicant who discloses the existence of a cartel before the DG report. Subsequent applicants can receive reductions up to 50% (second applicant) and up to 30% (third applicant) in order of their priority status, provided they offer continuous and complete co-operation.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 53A & 53B - Appeals to NCLAT under Competition Act
questions.question: Under the Competition Act, 2002, which appellate forum hears appeals against any direction, decision or order passed by the Competition Commission of India (CCI), and within what timeframe?
options: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), within 60 days from the date on which a copy of the direction, decision or order is received (with power to condone delay on sufficient cause).
The High Court of Delhi within 30 days.
The Supreme Court of India directly within 45 days.
The Securities Appellate Tribunal within 90 days.
questions.ref: Section 53A and Section 53B of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 53A, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) is the designated Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals against orders of the CCI. Under Section 53B(2), every appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date on which a copy of the direction, decision or order made by the Commission is received. Delay may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 48 - Offences and Contraventions by Companies
questions.question: Where an enterprise contravenes any of the provisions of the Competition Act, 2002, who is deemed to be guilty of the contravention under Section 48?
options: Every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business, as well as the company, unless he proves that the contravention was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence.
Only the Company Secretary who signed the board minutes.
All equity shareholders in proportion to their shareholding.
Only the independent directors on the Audit Committee.
questions.ref: Section 48(1) of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 48(1), where a person committing contravention of any of the provisions of this Act or of any rule, regulation, direction or order is a company, every person who, at the time the contravention was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the contravention and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 26 - Procedure for Inquiry on Complaints (Forming Prima Facie Opinion)
questions.question: Under Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, when an information is filed under Section 19 alleging contravention of Section 3 or 4, what action does the CCI take if it is of the opinion that there exists a prima facie case?
options: It shall direct the Director General (DG) to cause an investigation to be made into the matter.
It immediately passes a final cease-and-desist order without hearing.
It orders the immediate arrest of the Managing Director of the opposite party.
It transfers the matter to the local District Consumer Forum.
questions.ref: Section 26(1) of the Competition Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 26(1), on receipt of an information or reference from the Central Government or a State Government or on its own knowledge, if the Commission is of the opinion that there exists a prima facie case, it shall direct the Director General to cause an investigation to be made into the matter. If no prima facie case exists, it closes the matter under Section 26(2).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Competition Act, 2002
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 44 - Penalty for Making False Statement in Combinations
questions.question: If an enterprise filing a notice of combination under Section 6(2) makes a statement which is false in any material particular or omits to state any material fact knowing it to be material, what penalty is leviable under Section 44?
options: A penalty which shall not be less than ₹50 Lakhs but which may extend to ₹5 Crores.
A penalty of ₹10,000 only.
Imprisonment for 14 years without bail.
Automatic confiscation of all assets of the acquirer.
questions.ref: Section 44 of the Competition Act, 2002 (as amended)
questions.explanation: Under Section 44, if any person, being a party to a combination, makes a statement which is false in any material particular, or knowing it to be false, or omits to state any material particular knowing it to be material, such person shall be liable to a penalty which shall not be less than fifty lakh rupees but which may extend to five crore rupees.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 124 & 125 - Contract of Indemnity vs Guarantee
questions.question: Mr. Sharma enters into a contract with an insurance company promising to make good any loss suffered by the company due to an ongoing patent litigation by a rival firm. What is the fundamental statutory distinction between a contract of indemnity (Sec 124) and a contract of guarantee (Sec 126)?
options: A contract of indemnity involves two parties and primary liability arising on the happening of a contingency, whereas a contract of guarantee involves three parties (creditor, principal debtor, surety) with the surety's liability being secondary upon default of the principal debtor.
An indemnity requires three parties while a guarantee requires two parties.
A contract of guarantee must always be in writing while indemnity must be oral.
A surety in guarantee has no right of subrogation against the principal debtor.
questions.ref: Section 124 and Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 124, a contract of indemnity is a contract whereby one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor or by any other person (2 parties, 1 contract, primary liability). Under Section 126, a contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default (3 parties, 3 contracts, secondary/collateral liability).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 128 - Surety's Co-extensive Liability
questions.question: Bank of India grants a term loan of ₹50 Lakhs to Zen Infra Pvt. Ltd., secured by personal guarantee executed by Mr. Rakesh. Upon default by Zen Infra Pvt. Ltd., Bank of India files a recovery suit directly against guarantor Mr. Rakesh without first suing the principal debtor Zen Infra. Can Mr. Rakesh claim that the bank must exhaust its remedies against the principal debtor first?
options: No, under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor unless it is otherwise provided by the contract, enabling the creditor to proceed directly against the surety.
Yes, the creditor is legally bound to sell all assets of the principal debtor before touching the surety.
Yes, because a guarantor is only liable for 50% of the loan amount.
No, but the bank must obtain previous permission of the NCLT before suing a guarantor.
questions.ref: Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad)
questions.explanation: Under Section 128, the liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract. The creditor is not required to exhaust his remedies against the principal debtor before suing the surety (confirmed by Supreme Court in Bank of Bihar v. Damodar Prasad).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 133 - Discharge of Surety by Variance in Terms
questions.question: Mr. Verma stands surety to ABC Ltd. for the fidelity of Mr. Raman who is appointed as a cashier at a salary of ₹30,000 per month. Subsequently, without Mr. Verma's knowledge or consent, ABC Ltd. agrees to pay Raman on commission basis (which results in fluctuating income) and Raman is tasked with higher responsibilities. Raman misappropriates funds. Is Mr. Verma liable as surety under Section 133?
options: No, Mr. Verma is discharged as to transactions subsequent to the variance, because any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between principal debtor and creditor discharges the surety.
Yes, because the misappropriation occurred within the course of employment.
Yes, because variance in compensation does not affect the fidelity undertaking.
Mr. Verma is liable only to the extent of ₹30,000 per month.
questions.ref: Section 133 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 133, any variance, made without the surety's consent, in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor, discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance. The change in Raman's remuneration and role without Verma's consent completely discharges the surety.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 140 & 141 - Surety's Right of Subrogation & Securities
questions.question: Mr. Kishore stands surety for a bank loan of ₹20 Lakhs granted to Mr. Anuj. The bank also holds a mortgage over Anuj's commercial shop worth ₹15 Lakhs. Mr. Kishore pays the full ₹20 Lakhs to the bank on Anuj's default. What rights does Mr. Kishore have under Section 140 and Section 141?
options: Mr. Kishore is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor (Doctrine of Subrogation) and is entitled to the benefit of the mortgage over the shop, whether he knew of the security or not.
Mr. Kishore only has an unsecured personal claim against Anuj with no right over the mortgaged shop.
The mortgage over the shop gets extinguished automatically upon payment of debt.
The shop must be surrendered to the State Government.
questions.ref: Section 140 and Section 141 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 140 (Right of Subrogation), where a guaranteed debt has become due and the surety pays all that he is liable for, he is invested with all the rights which the creditor had against the principal debtor. Under Section 141, a surety is entitled to the benefit of every security which the creditor has against the principal debtor, whether the surety knew of the existence of such security or not.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 148 & 151 - Bailment & Bailee's Duty of Care
questions.question: Mr. Bajaj leaves his luxury car at a modern authorized service center for scheduled servicing. A flash fire breaks out in the adjacent paint booth due to defective electrical wiring installed by the service center without required safety circuit breakers. The car is completely destroyed. The service center points to a disclaimer printed on the job card: 'Goods parked and serviced at customer's own risk; management not liable for fire or theft.' What is the legal liability of the service center under Section 151 and 152?
options: The service center is liable for damages because under Section 151 the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed as a man of ordinary prudence would of his own goods, and a bailee cannot contract out of this minimum standard of care through an exemption clause where negligence is proved.
The disclaimer clause on the job card completely shields the service center from all liability.
The service center is only liable if the customer took out third-party fire insurance.
Under the Indian Contract Act, bailment does not apply to motor vehicle servicing.
questions.ref: Section 151 and Section 152 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 151, in all cases of bailment the bailee is bound to take as much care of the goods bailed to him as a man of ordinary prudence would, under similar circumstances, take of his own goods. It is well settled that a bailee cannot contract out of the minimum statutory duty of care under Section 151 where damage is caused by his own negligence.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 170 & 171 - Particular Lien vs General Lien
questions.question: Which of the following parties is entitled to a 'General Lien' under Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, allowing them to retain any goods bailed to them as a security for a general balance of account in the absence of a contract to the contrary?
options: Bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers.
Carpenters, tailors, and repairmen who have expended labor on specific goods.
All trade suppliers in wholesale commercial transactions.
Common carriers transporting agricultural produce.
questions.ref: Section 170 and Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 171, bankers, factors, wharfingers, attorneys of a High Court and policy-brokers may, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, retain as a security for a general balance of account, any goods bailed to them. All other bailees (such as repairers, mechanics, tailors) have only a 'Particular Lien' under Section 170 in respect of goods on which they have expended labor/skill.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 172 & 176 - Contract of Pledge & Pawnee's Rights on Default
questions.question: Mr. Kapoor pledges gold ornaments with a registered Non-Banking Financial Company (pawnee) as security for a loan of ₹5 Lakhs repayable in 6 months. Mr. Kapoor fails to repay on the due date. What legal remedies are available to the pawnee under Section 176?
options: The pawnee may bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt and retain the goods as a collateral security; OR he may sell the thing pledged on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale.
The pawnee becomes the absolute owner of the gold ornaments automatically upon default without giving any notice.
The pawnee cannot sell the pledged goods under any circumstances without obtaining a decree from a civil court.
The pawnee must refund 50% of the gold ornaments to the borrower.
questions.ref: Section 176 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 176, if the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt at the stipulated time, the pawnee may: (a) bring a suit against the pawnor upon the debt or promise, and retain the goods pledged as a collateral security; OR (b) sell the thing pledged, on giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale. If proceeds are less than debt, pawnor is liable for balance; if surplus, pawnee pays surplus to pawnor.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 182 & 186 - Creation of Agency & Express/Implied Authority
questions.question: A merchant in Kolkata employs an agent in Mumbai to purchase cotton. The agent purchases cotton on credit in his own name without disclosing that he is acting for a principal. Under Section 231 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what are the rights of the seller and the undisclosed principal?
options: If the principal discloses himself before the contract is completed, the other contracting party may refuse to fulfill the contract if he can show that he would not have entered into it with the principal; otherwise, the principal may require the performance of the contract, and the third party can sue either the agent or the principal.
The contract is completely void because agency requires disclosure of principal at the inception.
Only the agent is liable; the principal can never sue or be sued on undisclosed contracts.
The seller must file a criminal case for impersonation against the agent.
questions.ref: Section 231 and Section 233 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 231, if an agent makes a contract with a person who neither knows, nor has reason to suspect, that he is an agent, his principal may require the performance of the contract. Under Section 233, in cases where the agent is personally liable, a person dealing with him may hold either him or his principal, or both of them, liable.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 201 & 202 - Agency Coupled with Interest (Irrevocable Agency)
questions.question: Mr. Mohan borrows ₹10 Lakhs from Mr. Naresh and appoints Mr. Naresh as his attorney to collect rents from Mohan's commercial complex and adjust the collected rents against the outstanding loan until full repayment. Mohan subsequently issues a notice revoking the power of attorney. Can Mohan legally revoke this agency under Section 202?
options: No, where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest.
Yes, a principal has absolute right to revoke any power of attorney at any time.
Yes, provided Mohan pays a cancellation penalty of ₹50,000 to the sub-registrar.
The agency terminates automatically on the expiry of 1 year.
questions.ref: Section 202 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
questions.explanation: Under Section 202 (Termination of agency where agent has an interest in subject-matter), where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest, nor does it terminate upon the death or insanity of the principal. This is an irrevocable agency.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 73 - Compensation for Loss or Damage Caused by Breach
questions.question: A textile mill contracted to supply industrial fabric to a garment exporter by August 10. The mill failed to deliver. The exporter had entered into a lucrative export contract with a French buyer, which was cancelled, resulting in huge loss of extraordinary profits. The exporter had not informed the mill about the French contract at the time of entering into the supply contract. Can the exporter recover this special loss of profits under Section 73 (Hadley v. Baxendale rule)?
options: No, compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage; special damages can only be claimed if the special circumstances leading to such loss were brought to the knowledge of the mill at the time of making the contract.
Yes, all losses whether direct, indirect, remote or speculative are recoverable upon breach of commercial contracts.
Yes, but only if the exporter obtains a certificate of damages from a Chartered Accountant.
The exporter can recover 50% of the French contract profits under the rule of equity.
questions.ref: Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Hadley v. Baxendale)
questions.explanation: Under Section 73, compensation is payable for loss or damage which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach. Compensation is not payable for remote and indirect losses. Special damages for loss of the French contract cannot be recovered because the special circumstances were never communicated to the supplier.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Indian Contract Act, 1872, and related economic laws
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Sec 74 - Liquidated Damages vs Penalty
questions.question: A software development contract specifies that in case of any delay beyond December 31, the developer shall pay liquidated damages of ₹10,000 per day of delay. The developer delays completion by 20 days. Under Section 74, what amount is the aggrieved client entitled to receive from the Court?
options: Reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount of ₹10,000 per day (the stipulated amount), whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby.
The entire contract price becomes forfeited automatically.
Double the stipulated amount as punitive damages.
Zero compensation unless the client proves actual cash losses with bank receipts.
questions.ref: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass / Maula Bux)
questions.explanation: Under Section 74, when a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of breach, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 2(7) - Consumer Definition & Commercial Purpose Exclusion
questions.question: Apex Heavy Machinery Pvt. Ltd. purchases an industrial generator costing ₹35 Lakhs for use in its automotive manufacturing plant. The generator breaks down repeatedly due to manufacturing defects. Apex Heavy Machinery files a complaint before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Can Apex Heavy Machinery maintain the complaint as a 'consumer'?
options: No, because under Section 2(7) of CPA 2019, a person who obtains goods for 'commercial purpose' is excluded from the definition of a consumer (unless purchased exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment).
Yes, any entity that pays consideration is unconditionally a consumer under CPA 2019.
Yes, provided the complaint is supported by a technical engineer's affidavit.
Companies are never permitted to file consumer complaints under any circumstances.
questions.ref: Section 2(7)(i) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Under Section 2(7)(i) of CPA 2019, 'consumer' means any person who buys any goods for a consideration, but DOES NOT INCLUDE a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose. Under the Explanation, 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment. An industrial company purchasing machinery for manufacturing is excluded.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 - Pecuniary Jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions
questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021, what are the pecuniary jurisdictions of the District Commission, State Commission, and National Commission based on value of goods/services paid as consideration?
options: District Commission: Value up to ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission: Value exceeding ₹50 Lakhs up to ₹2 Crores; National Commission: Value exceeding ₹2 Crores.
District: up to ₹1 Crore; State: ₹1 Cr to ₹10 Cr; National: above ₹10 Cr.
District: up to ₹20 Lakhs; State: ₹20 Lakhs to ₹1 Cr; National: above ₹1 Cr.
District: up to ₹5 Lakhs; State: ₹5 Lakhs to ₹50 Lakhs; National: above ₹50 Lakhs.
questions.ref: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commission) Rules, 2021 (Notification dated 30.12.2021)
questions.explanation: By the 2021 Rules revising pecuniary jurisdiction under CPA 2019: District Commission entertains complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission where consideration exceeds ₹50 Lakhs but does not exceed ₹2 Crores; National Commission where consideration exceeds ₹2 Crores.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 82 to 87 - Product Liability
questions.question: A consumer purchases a pressure cooker from an authorized retail shop. Due to a defect in the safety valve manufactured with substandard alloy, the cooker explodes, causing severe burn injuries to the consumer and property damage to the kitchen. Under Chapter VI (Product Liability) of CPA, 2019, who can be held liable in a product liability action?
options: A product liability action may be brought against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product under Section 82.
Only the retail shopkeeper who handed the box to the customer.
No product liability action can be initiated unless criminal charges of murder are framed.
Liability is limited strictly to the replacement of the pressure cooker with no damages for physical harm.
questions.ref: Section 82, 84 and 86 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Under Section 82 of CPA 2019, a product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer or a product service provider or a product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product. Under Section 84, a product manufacturer is liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, or lacks adequate instructions/warnings.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 10 & 21 - CCPA Powers & Celebrity Endorsement Liability
questions.question: Under Section 10 and 21 of CPA, 2019, what power does the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) possess regarding misleading advertisements and celebrity endorsers?
options: CCPA can direct withdrawal/modification of misleading ads, impose penalties up to ₹10 Lakhs (and up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent contravention) on manufacturers/endorsers, and prohibit an endorser from endorsing that product/service for up to 1 year (extendable up to 3 years).
CCPA can only issue non-binding recommendations to the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI).
Celebrity endorsers have absolute statutory immunity from prosecution.
CCPA can revoke the citizenship of celebrity endorsers.
questions.ref: Section 21(1), 21(2) and 21(3) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Under Section 21 of CPA 2019, the CCPA may impose a penalty up to ₹10 Lakhs on a manufacturer or endorser for false/misleading advertisement (up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent violations), and prohibit the endorser of a false or misleading advertisement from making endorsement of any product or service for a period which may extend to one year (up to 3 years for subsequent violations). Endorser is exempt if he carried out due diligence.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 69 - Limitation Period for Filing Complaint
questions.question: Under Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what is the limitation period within which a complaint must be filed before the District Commission, State Commission, or National Commission?
options: Within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen (condonable if sufficient cause is shown).
Within one year from the date of purchase of the product.
Within 90 days from the date of issuing notice to the seller.
Within 3 years as per the general Limitation Act, 1963.
questions.ref: Section 69(1) and 69(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Under Section 69(1), the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Under Section 69(2), a complaint may be entertained after two years if the complainant satisfies the Commission that he had sufficient cause for not filing within period.

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 41, 51 & 67 - Appeals & Pre-Deposit Requirement
questions.question: An order is passed by the State Commission directing a builder to refund ₹80 Lakhs to a homebuyer. The builder intends to file an appeal before the National Commission under Section 51. What pre-deposit condition must the builder satisfy before the appeal can be entertained?
options: The builder must deposit fifty percent (50%) of the amount ordered by the State Commission before the National Commission can entertain the appeal.
Deposit of ₹25,000 only.
Deposit of 100% of the awarded amount plus interest.
Zero deposit is required for filing an appeal under CPA 2019.
questions.ref: Second proviso to Section 51(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
questions.explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 51(1), no appeal by a person who is required to pay any amount in terms of an order of the State Commission shall be entertained by the National Commission unless the appellant has deposited fifty per cent (50%) of that amount in the prescribed manner. Similar 50% pre-deposit rules apply to appeals from District to State Commission (Sec 41) and from National Commission to Supreme Court (Sec 67).

questions.subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
questions.topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 3 & 4 - Offence of Money Laundering & Punishment
questions.question: Under Section 3 and 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party in any process connected with the proceeds of crime is guilty of money laundering. What is the statutory punishment prescribed under Section 4?
options: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 3 years but which may extend to 7 years (and up to 10 years if the scheduled offence is under the NDPS Act) and fine.
Simple imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to ₹1 Lakh.
Monetary fine only with zero prison sentence.
Detention in civil prison for 6 months.
questions.ref: Section 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 4, any person who commits the offence of money-laundering shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine. Where the proceeds of crime involved relate to any offence specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule (NDPS Act), the imprisonment may extend to ten years.

questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 5 - Attachment of Property Involved in Money Laundering
questions.question: Under Section 5(1) of PMLA, 2002, the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director may provisionally attach property involved in money laundering. What is the maximum validity period of such provisional attachment order before confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority?
options: For a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order.
For a period of 30 days only.
For 1 year automatically.
Indefinitely until completion of criminal trial.
questions.ref: Section 5(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 5(1), where the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director has reason to believe that any person is in possession of proceeds of crime, he may by order in writing provisionally attach such property for a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order. The attachment must be confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8.

questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 12 - Reporting Entities & Client Verification (KYC)
questions.question: Under Section 12 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, every reporting entity (including banking companies, financial institutions, intermediaries, and designated professionals) must maintain records of all transactions for what minimum duration?
options: For a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity, and maintain records of identity of clients for five years after the business relationship has ended.
For a period of two years from the audit date.
For eight years under the Companies Act rules.
Records must be permanently preserved indefinitely.
questions.ref: Section 12(1)(a) and Section 12(3) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
questions.explanation: Under Section 12(3) of PMLA, records of transactions referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) shall be maintained for a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity. Under Section 12(4), records of identity of clients and account files shall be maintained for a period of five years after the business relationship has ended or account closed.

questions.tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 24 - Burden of Proof in Money Laundering
questions.question: Under Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, in any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime, upon whom does the burden of proof lie with respect to property being untainted?
options: In the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering, and the burden of proving that the property is untainted lies on the accused.
The prosecution (Enforcement Directorate) must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt without any statutory presumption.
The burden of proof shifts to the commercial bank where funds were deposited.
Burden of proof lies on the statutory auditor who certified the balance sheet.
questions.ref: Section 24(a) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. UOI)
questions.explanation: Under Section 24(a) of PMLA, 2002, in the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering. The burden of proof is reversed and placed on the accused to establish that the property is untainted (upheld by Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary).
